### How threads and machines work together

- **Two thread homes, never bi-directionally merged:**
  - **Standalone local thread** (unauthenticated or explicitly local-only on desktop): lives in local SQLite + local disk. Works offline with zero server. Optional one-way **Publish to cloud** uploads its event log and blobs to the Control Plane and hands off to a cloud thread.
  - **Cloud/team thread** (default when signed into a company workspace): ledger always lives in Control Plane Postgres and attachments/files live in S3. Readable and actionable from Desktop, Web, and iOS at all times.
- **Per-turn execution target (no stuck threads):**
  - Any turn on a cloud thread executes on either the user's **Cloud Sandbox** (default) or a **Connected Machine** (the user's online desktop or a registered office workstation).
  - Consecutive turns on the same target resume the provider's native ACP session directly.
  - Switching target (e.g. Turn 1 on laptop, Turn 2 from iOS on a train) triggers an explicit **checkpoint handoff**: the new target starts a fresh native ACP session seeded with a structured handoff (recent transcript + summary + S3 workspace/blob refs + memory refs) while appending to the **same** Jaz thread in Postgres. No forked chats, no stranded history.
- **Connected machines built on Jaz's existing `desktopbridge`:**
  - Jaz already implements outbound WebSocket JSON-RPC from Electron desktop to backend (`backend/internal/desktopbridge/connection.go`, `browsercontrol/desktop_host.go`, `computercontrol/connection.go`).
  - Generalize this into **`machinebridge`**: an online desktop app (or headless `jaz-node` daemon on an office Windows/Linux box) holds one outbound TLS WebSocket to the Control Plane — zero inbound ports, works cleanly behind corporate NAT/VPNs.
  - The user locally approves explicit capabilities per machine: `fs` (strictly scoped to allowed directories, e.g. `~/Tenders` or a mapped NAS share), `browser` (existing side-browser control), `computer` (existing native desktop control), and optionally `exec` (running full local turns).
  - **Default pattern for enterprise teams (Tool Target, not Remote Control):** The turn runs in the Cloud Sandbox and calls scoped MCP tools (`machine_fs_list`, `machine_fs_read`, `machine_stage_file`) through `machinebridge`. Any file pulled from the laptop is immediately cached into the thread's S3 prefix — so closing the laptop mid-run never breaks the cloud agent.

## 3. Kubernetes `agent-sandbox` on cloud and bare metal

Using [`kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox`](https://agent-sandbox.sigs.k8s.io/docs/) gives one standard orchestrator for EKS/AKS/GKE and single-node bare-metal `k3s`:

- **Primitives used:**
  - `SandboxTemplate`: generic base image containing managed agent CLIs, Python/Office tools for plugins, and a small bootstrapper that pulls/verifies the pinned `jaz` binary hash (so runtime upgrades rarely require rebuilding base images).
  - `SandboxWarmPool`: keeps N pre-booted, unclaimed pods warm (zero tenant data attached) for sub-second `SandboxClaim` allocation.
  - `SandboxClaim`: **one ephemeral sandbox per active user** (not per thread). A user working across three tender threads reuses one warm pod and hot file cache instead of paying three cold starts. When a second teammate takes over a shared thread, their own sandbox hydrates that thread's S3 workspace — users never share a container or filesystem.
  - `SandboxRouter`: Control Plane proxies sandbox RPC/streams through the router using `X-Sandbox-ID` / `X-Sandbox-Namespace`, avoiding raw Pod IP exposure.
- **Runtime isolation:**
  - **Cloud VMs (EKS/AKS/GKE):** `gVisor` (`runsc`) via `RuntimeClass` (works without nested KVM).
  - **Bare-metal Linux / metal instances:** `Kata Containers` (hardware KVM microVM per user) or `gVisor`.
- **Critical caveat — do not rely on VM memory snapshots:**
  - Full memory/register Pod Snapshots in `agent-sandbox` are currently GKE-specific; upstream bare-metal pause stops the pod while keeping its PVC.
  - **Design around this:** treat sandboxes as 100% disposable compute. Hydrate thread workspace files from S3 on claim/resume (or local NVMe cache + S3 sync), flush diffs on turn completion with optimistic `generation` numbers (preventing a stale pod from overwriting a newer run), reap idle ACP child processes aggressively (measured at 740–940 MB per open agent session), and scale idle pods to zero (short timeout ~5 min with no client attached, ~20 min while watched).
- **Keep a small `SandboxDriver` interface in Go:**
  - `Acquire(ctx, userID)`, `Endpoint(ctx, lease)`, `Release(ctx, lease)`.
  - Production driver: `K8sAgentSandboxDriver`. Local dev / tiny single-host driver: `DockerPodmanDriver` (making it easy to test locally or fold in existing Podman isolation work without requiring a local K8s cluster).

## 4. Abstracted `BlobStore` (S3) for attachments, plugins, and workspaces

Today Jaz scatters files across four local-disk assumptions: `.jaz-attachments/` (`backend/internal/server/attachment_store.go`), raw `media.Ref.BlobPath` (`backend/internal/media/ref.go`), `view-state/` (`backend/internal/plugins/views.go`), and thread working folders read directly by `plugins/page.go`.

Unify all four behind one `internal/blobstore` interface with two implementations:
- **`LocalFSBlobStore`** — standalone desktop mode (zero external dependencies).
- **`S3BlobStore`** — any S3-compatible store (AWS S3, GCS S3-interop, Azure Blob S3 gateway, or **MinIO / RustFS** inside bare-metal `k3s`).

### S3 key layout and Postgres index

| Bucket prefix | Contents | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tenants/<tid>/blobs/<sha256>` | Immutable attachments & media (`att:<blob_id>`) | Content-addressed dedupe (200-page tender packs uploaded once); works identically in cloud sandboxes and local desktop cache |
| `tenants/<tid>/threads/<id>/files/<relpath>` | Tracked thread workspace files (`status.json`, `query-sheet.xlsx`, buyer PDFs/DOCX) + manifest generation | Opening the **Tenders** sidebar page or viewing a linked PDF/DOCX in the side panel serves straight from S3 + Postgres with **zero sandbox cold start** |
| `tenants/<tid>/threads/<id>/view-state/<plugin>/<view>/<file>.json` | Saved plugin review state (200 KB cap, `If-Match` versioned) | Multiple teammates reviewing/approving tender queries cannot silently overwrite each other |
| `tenants/<tid>/artifacts/<id>/v<N>` | Versioned standalone documents, canvases, HTML widgets | ACL-controlled sharing independent of thread lifecycle |
| `tenants/<tid>/memory/<scope>/...` | Markdown memory pages (`users/<uid>`, `spaces/<sid>`, `org`) | Human-readable, versioned, auditable, immediately synced on correction |

**Client upload/download path:** Desktop, Web, and Mobile never push large attachments through the Go API memory or leak client-local paths into prompts. Clients request a short-lived presigned upload URL from the Control Plane, upload straight to S3, and attach the resulting `blob_id` to the prompt. Local runs on a signed-in desktop fetch `blob_id` into a local content cache on demand.

## 5. Team memory, team threads, and enterprise plugins

### Three-tier memory scope (`jazmem`)

Extend `backend/internal/memoryservice` so cloud/team mode routes `memory_search` and `memory_get_page` through a **Scoped Memory Router** in the Control Plane, enforcing verified OIDC user/group claims server-side (never trusting sandbox input):

| Scope | Read access | Write policy | Connector ingestion | Example (manufacturing / tenders) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Personal (`user:<uid>`)** | User only (local + cloud) | User's threads + personal `dream` (plus opt-in one-way Mac upload) | User's Gmail/Outlook, Zoom, WhatsApp | Personal notes, drafting style, private follow-ups |
| **Team Space (`space:<sid>`)** | Space members (e.g. `DC Tenders`, `Non-DC Tenders`, `West Sales`) | **Shared-space threads or explicit "Save to team memory" only** — private threads never auto-write here | Shared mailboxes, space-scoped Salesforce/SharePoint folders | Past buyer query rulings, consultant preferences, regional positions |
| **Org (`org:<tid>`)** | All org users (or role-filtered) | Curators/admins only (or PR-style approval from agents; mirrorable from Git/SharePoint) | Approved company repositories / ERP read-only feeds | Product matrix, 40 engine data sheets, standard deviations, common remarks |

- **Propagation of fixes & deletions:** Every memory page stays Markdown in S3 with a revision row in Postgres. Correcting a data-sheet value or deleting a stale deviation immediately re-indexes that scope across the entire company with a full audit trail (`who`, `when`, `source thread`).
- **Response attribution:** `memory_search` queries `[personal, active_space, org]` in parallel and tags every returned citation with its scope (`[Personal]`, `[Space: DC Tenders]`, `[Org]`) so agents never confuse a private note with an approved company spec.

### Team threads and plugin pages

- **Visibility:** `Private` (default), `Shared` (explicit teammates/link), or `Space` (visible in the Space sidebar and aggregated into Space plugin pages).
- **Concurrency:** Many live SSE observers, **one active turn writer** enforced atomically by `ClaimTurn` in Postgres. Every message stores `author_user_id` (already started in migration `0075_message_authorship.sql`). Teammates can watch live, submit the next turn when idle, review/approve plugin views (`If-Match` optimistic locking on `view-state`), or click **Fork** (cheap pointer to parent event seq + copy-on-write S3 workspace manifest).
- **Team plugin pages:** `backend/internal/plugins/page.go` swaps its local disk scan (`os.OpenRoot`) for a `PageDataSource` backed by Postgres + S3 `status.json`. Opening **Tenders** shows every live tender in the rep's spaces instantaneously without booting sandboxes.
- **White-labeling & enterprise governance:**
  - Control Plane serves an org bootstrap payload at OIDC sign-in: custom branding (name/logo/accent for Web/Desktop/iOS), **pinned Company Plugin Catalogue** (auto-synced into every sandbox and client), approved models/agents, and an **IT kill switch** (per-connector read/write toggles + instant revocation).
  - **Commercial critical path (independent of K8s):** Enterprise customers on Microsoft 365 Copilot will require **Microsoft Entra ID** OIDC plus **Outlook, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams** connectors (plus Salesforce/SAP read-only MCPs). Placing connectors in the Control Plane means building each enterprise connector once with centralized OAuth admin consent and audit logging.

## 6. What to borrow (and skip) from `herdrdev/herdr`

Source review of [`herdrdev/herdr`](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr) highlights five patterns worth adopting directly and two that do not fit Jaz:

| Pattern in `herdr` | Source reference | How Jaz should apply it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Frozen capability-negotiated endpoint envelope** | `src/protocol/endpoint.rs` (`endpoint.hello.v1` / `welcome.v1`, `capabilities`, `Unknown` enum fallbacks) | Version `machinebridge` and client-gateway handshakes with capability lists so desktop clients, `jaz-node` hosts, and cloud sandboxes upgrade independently instead of lockstep (`docs/remote-backend.md`). |
| **Multi-endpoint multiplexing with interest gating & isolated failure** | `src/client/endpoint/message_policy.rs`, `docs/connecting-machines.mdx` | Desktop connects to Local Runtime + Company Cloud simultaneously. Local opens immediately offline; background threads/endpoints receive lightweight status (`working`/`asking`/`idle`) until opened; an offline cloud or machine dims cached state without blocking local work. |
| **Sleep-aware application heartbeats** | `src/client/endpoint/health.rs` (60s startup window vs 5s/10s live probe, immediate reprobe on wake, idle bridge cleanup) | Upgrade `desktopbridge.KeepAlive` (currently a blind 25s ping / 75s read deadline) so `machinebridge` detects lid-close, VPN resets, and office Wi-Fi drops cleanly without killing cloud runs. |
| **Transparent local asset bridging on paste/drop** | `src/client/clipboard_images.rs` | Intercept pasted images and dragged local files in Desktop/Web/Mobile and upload them directly to `BlobStore` with size limits — never sending local paths to a remote turn. |
| **Single controller vs multiple observers & durable/transient split** | `src/handoff_runtime.rs`, `docs/persistence-remote.mdx` | Match team thread semantics: one turn-writer lease, unlimited live SSE observers, and explicit separation of durable state (Postgres + S3) from transient streams recreated on reconnect. |

**Do not copy from `herdr`:**
- **SSH-initiated remote connections:** assumes developer SSH keys and inbound host reachability; non-technical enterprise teams behind corporate firewalls need OIDC + outbound TLS WebSockets.
- **PTY / OSC 7501 terminal scraping:** Jaz already owns structured ACP/native typed `sessionevents`, which power mobile UI, plugin views, and audit logs cleanly.

## 7. Phased build order

1. **Phase 1 — Runtime storage & blob interfaces (no behavior change locally):**

   - Add Postgres implementation of `storage.Store` alongside SQLite (same event schema).
   - Add `worker` runtime mode flags (`--control-plane-url`, short-lived JWT auth, workspace S3 sync on turn boundaries).
2. **Phase 2 — Control plane + K8s `agent-sandbox` + team threads:**

   - Generalize `desktopbridge` with `herdr`-style capability negotiation and sleep-aware health probes.

## Proposed changes

Sizes are estimates.

### 1. Follow the app standard (done)

- [x] **Tell servers Jaz can show views.** The standard requires the feature to be negotiated, and its server kit registers a text-only tool when the client does not declare it ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). Jaz creates all three of its clients with no options, so it never declares it: [`mcp.go:524`](../backend/internal/mcp/mcp.go), [`mcp.go:565`](../backend/internal/mcp/mcp.go), [`stdio.go:23`](../backend/internal/mcp/stdio.go). Servers that follow the standard give Jaz no views. One shared options value fixes it.
- [x] **Enforce each view's network policy.** The standard says the host must build the policy from the domains a view declares and block everything when none are declared ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). `ReadApp` returns only the HTML and drops that declaration ([`apps.go:153`](../backend/internal/mcp/apps.go)), and the frame loads the HTML as is ([`MCPAppFrame.tsx:197`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/components/apps/MCPAppFrame.tsx)). Jaz's own generated artifacts are locked down ([`artifacts.ts:16`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/lib/artifacts.ts)); third-party view code is not. CRM already declares "no network connections" and Jaz ignores it.

### 2. Connect views to the conversation (done)

- [x] **Let a view post into its thread.** The standard's `ui/message` request sends a user message and starts a turn ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). Jaz advertises only links, tool calls and logging ([`MCPAppFrame.tsx:165`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/components/apps/MCPAppFrame.tsx)). Artifacts in the same transcript row can already send a prompt ([`LiveEvent.tsx:59`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/components/session/LiveEvent.tsx)); app views should use that same path, with the existing "only the view in use" focus check.
- [x] **Let a view tell the model what the user did.** `ui/update-model-context` carries a selection or draft to the model with the next message, without starting a turn ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). Send it as its own typed block on the next turn, never by rewriting the prompt text.
- [x] **Tell panel and inline views which thread they are in.** A panel view gets no thread and no size ([`SidePanel.tsx:107`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/components/session/SidePanel.tsx), [`mcpAppHost.ts:24`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/lib/mcpAppHost.ts)). Add the thread and the container size to the host context. Reporting a panel as "fullscreen" is fine: the standard has only inline, fullscreen and picture-in-picture.
- [x] **Let a card expand.** Answer `ui/request-display-mode` by opening the same call in the side panel, so a long form is not squeezed into the chat column.

# Proposal: a tenders plugin for Sterling Green in Jaz

Build it as a plugin: a folder of skills, a few views and one script, kept in a Sterling Green repository and installed into Jaz from there. The skills turn a tender folder into three files in the thread's folder: a tender brief, a query sheet the rep edits in the side panel, and an Excel file in the buyer's template. Jaz already has most of what this needs; five gaps are listed below. The repository and a first version of the plugin now exist. A dedicated review screen, as in the earlier mocks, comes after the trial and only if the document proves too slow to check.

## What the sample data shows

The folder holds two real purchase-stage packs with the sheets that were sent, and the team's check-points sheet ([sample folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1J6NjopLQUjPFOCfe0wEAOPUnLN1pNSwh)).

- **A query sheet is one row per point, with a column per round.** Adani's has 44 points, each with the document, clause, the buyer's clause text and the query, then Adani's response, Sterling's reply of 9 Feb and the meeting minutes of 20 Feb ([Adani sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Hcy8ysTe4ifPiQ9ZDKx6KZA5O2FE6gIv)).
- **The buyer sets the format.** PDG's sheet is PDG's own form, "Addendum to RFP" IMS-TPL-PRC-19, with different columns ([PDG sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fwUlR5Fi52YDVkHpNLEEq7DVPXGVYHnS)). The export has to fill the buyer's file, not ours.
- **Open points are repeated in later rounds.** PDG's sheet has 132 rows, but the load-bank point appears three times (rows 33, 45 and 129), each with a newer reply ([PDG sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fwUlR5Fi52YDVkHpNLEEq7DVPXGVYHnS)). Round handling is part of the job, not an extra.
- **Half the points do not come from the specification.** In Adani's sheet 19 of 44 points cite the price schedule, 13 the generator specification and 6 the commissioning summary. In PDG's, 63 of 132 cite the special conditions, 15 the test scripts and 7 the bill of quantities (counted from both sheets). Reading only the specification PDF would miss about half.
- **The check-points sheet is the method.** It lists 77 points in 12 categories with Sterling's "Offered Specification" filled in and a "Tender Requirement" column left empty for each tender ([Standard Check Points](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1u1aS8YvSR1mAXKZH8J133pblwwZ_wTWM)).   - Insulation class H where class F was asked (check points 32–33, PDG point 13).

  - 25 dB insertion loss against a 75 dB(A) limit (check point 40, Adani point 3).
- **Points fall into five kinds** (my reading of both sheets):
  - a deviation that states our standard;
  - a scope question;
  - a document the tender refers to but did not include;
  - a contradiction between two documents;
  - a commercial term passed to procurement.
- **Not in the sample:** the product matrix, data sheets, the common-remarks sheet, lead-stage sheets and any non-data-centre pack, all promised on the 13 Nov call ([16:06 session](https://notes.granola.ai/d/e4e8b0d2-6083-483f-ac88-4bf6ecf774a5)).

A fresh agent followed `query-sheet` on each sample pack without seeing the sheet that was sent, and each draft was then compared with that sheet (drafts and comparisons are in the repository's ignored `runs/` folder).

|---|---|---|

## The document on the right

Use a Markdown document in Jaz's editable reader, with one section per point instead of one wide table. Excel stays the delivery format and is generated from the document.

```markdown

> Supply, installation, testing and commissioning of 990 liters double skin
> day tank … as shown in P&ID drawing

**Query:** Please share the P&ID drawing so we can count the level

It is the better review tool, but it is a separate app to build and host, with its own database of tenders, the way Jaz CRM and Jaz Tasks are separate apps that Jaz connects to. ## How a plugin works in Jaz

This part is built on the task branch and not yet merged or released.

**A plugin is a folder.** The [author guide](plugins.md) defines the current Agent Plugins manifest, native manifest fallbacks, skills, views, and optional Jaz page. Jaz keeps installed plugins in `~/.jaz/plugins` and offers their skills to every agent, beside the user's own ([`plugins.go`](../backend/internal/plugins/plugins.go), [`skills.go`](../backend/internal/skills/skills.go)).

**A skill shows a view by name.** The agent has one new tool, `show_view`, and passes a view's name and what to draw, never the HTML ([`tools.go`](../backend/internal/plugins/tools.go)):

| Call | Where it appears |
|---|---|
| `view`, `data: {…}` | A card in the conversation |
| `view`, `file: "status.json"` | A tab in the side panel that opens by itself when the skill shows it and redraws whenever the file changes, without reloading ([`ViewPanel.tsx`](../frontend/src/renderer/src/components/session/ViewPanel.tsx)) |

The tenders plugin has one view, `tenders/status`, in the side panel. It leads with the one thing the rep has to do now, lists the points waiting for them, and keeps the stages of the work and the documents below. Questions to the rep use Jaz's own question card, not a view.

A view runs in Jaz's existing sandboxed frame with the app's colours and fonts. It reads `window.data`, hears later versions through `window.onData`, sends a message to the thread with `sendPrompt` and opens a file from the thread's folder beside itself with `openLink`.

**The flow for a tender:**

1. The rep starts a thread, attaches the tender folder and asks for the query sheet.
2. The skill reads the pack and shows the status view. It stays in the side panel for the rest of the work.
3. The skill fills the check points and drafts `query-sheet.md`. After each step it reruns `status.py`, and the view moves on.
4. For each point that needs a decision, the skill asks with Jaz's question card. The rep clicks an answer, or opens the query sheet from the status view and edits it directly.
5. The status view's one button asks for the next step: export to Excel, read the buyer's replies, prepare the bid.

# Releasing Jaz

Bump the version, update [`RELEASE-NOTES.md`](RELEASE-NOTES.md), commit both and push the matching `v` tag. That triggers
[`Release`](../.github/workflows/release-desktop.yml), which creates a draft,
builds and uploads all artifacts, then publishes it as the latest release
only after every build succeeds. The previous complete release stays available
to updaters while the new build runs.

The tag must equal `frontend/package.json` version with a `v` prefix
(`0.0.11` → `v0.0.11`), or the build fails.

```sh
# Bump frontend/package.json and update docs/RELEASE-NOTES.md first.
git add frontend/package.json docs/RELEASE-NOTES.md
git commit -m "Release v0.0.11" -- frontend/package.json docs/RELEASE-NOTES.md
git push origin main

# Start the release build from that exact commit.
git tag v0.0.11
git push origin v0.0.11

# Watch the build.
gh run watch "$(gh run list --workflow=release-desktop.yml -L1 --json databaseId -q '.[0].databaseId')"
```

The workflow uploads macOS `*.dmg`, macOS/Windows `*.zip`, Windows `*.exe`,
`latest-mac.yml`, `latest.yml`, Linux/macOS `jaz-backend-<os>-<arch>.tar.gz`
backend assets, and matching `.sha256` files to the draft release. Retry failed
jobs with `gh run rerun <run-id> --failed`; uploads replace their earlier assets.
Never publish the draft manually before its builds finish.

Standalone backend release assets are built with version metadata. After
installing one, `/opt/jaz/bin/jaz --version` should print the release tag.

Desktop telemetry is enabled only when the release build receives
`POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN` as a repository variable or secret. The token is a
public PostHog project token. The capture host is hardcoded to
`https://us.i.posthog.com`.

# Remote Backend

Jaz can run with the backend on a server and desktop, browser, or mobile clients on user devices. The backend owns sessions, memory, tools, credentials, workspaces, and connected-device policy. Clients are control surfaces.

## Server Setup

Install a release backend on a Linux server:

```sh
ssh root@SERVER

apt-get update
apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl tar nodejs npm

useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/jaz --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin jaz || true
install -d -o root -g root -m 755 /opt/jaz/bin /etc/jaz
install -d -o jaz -g jaz -m 755 /var/lib/jaz /var/lib/jaz/workspaces/default

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$tmp"
arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture)
case "$arch" in amd64|arm64) ;; *) echo "unsupported architecture: $arch"; exit 1;; esac
asset="jaz-backend-linux-${arch}.tar.gz"
base=https://github.com/gluonfield/jaz/releases/latest/download
curl -fsSLO "$base/$asset"
curl -fsSLO "$base/$asset.sha256"
test "$(awk '{print $1}' "$asset.sha256")" = "$(sha256sum "$asset" | awk '{print $1}')"
tar -xzf "$asset"
install -o root -g root -m 755 jaz /opt/jaz/bin/jaz
```

`releases/latest/download` always resolves to the newest release, so this recipe
stays current without editing. To pin a specific release instead, swap in

`base=https://github.com/gluonfield/jaz/releases/download/v0.0.46`.

### Remote web previews

Agent-started web servers bind to the backend machine, so remote clients must never open their own `localhost`. Jaz registers loopback-only targets through the authenticated `POST /v1/preview/proxies` endpoint and returns a random, eight-hour capability URL on an isolated origin. The capability host forwards ordinary HTTP methods and WebSocket upgrades used by development servers such as Vite. Jaz strips Authorization, cookies, device headers, Origin, and Referer before the request reaches the preview process.

Set `--preview-url-template` to an origin containing `{id}` exactly once in its hostname, for example:

```text
https://{id}.preview.example.com
```

The template is explicit: Jaz never derives it from `--public-url`. It must use HTTP or HTTPS and cannot contain credentials, a path, query, or fragment. A remote backend without this setting rejects preview registration with an actionable error. Local Electron development keeps working without it through isolated `jaz-preview-<id>.localhost` origins.

The deployment must provide all of the following for the template:

- Wildcard DNS for `*.preview.example.com` pointing to the same reverse proxy or tunnel as the Jaz backend.
- A TLS certificate covering `*.preview.example.com` when the template uses HTTPS.
- A wildcard virtual-host or tunnel ingress rule that forwards the hostname unchanged to the Jaz backend.
- HTTP upgrade forwarding so preview WebSockets and Vite HMR reach Jaz's reverse proxy.

For a locally managed Cloudflare Tunnel, the matching ingress shape is:

```yaml
ingress:
  - hostname: jaz.example.com
    service: http://localhost:5299
  - hostname: "*.preview.example.com"
    service: http://localhost:5299
  - service: http_status:404
```

Create a proxied wildcard DNS record for `*.preview.example.com` targeting the tunnel, and ensure Cloudflare edge certificate coverage includes that exact wildcard. Then validate routing before restarting `cloudflared`:

```sh
cloudflared tunnel ingress validate
cloudflared tunnel ingress rule https://0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef.preview.example.com/.well-known/jaz-preview
dig +short 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef.preview.example.com
curl -i https://0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef.preview.example.com/.well-known/jaz-preview
```

The rule command must select the wildcard Jaz service, DNS must resolve, and HTTPS must complete without a certificate error. An unregistered hostname may be rejected by Jaz authentication, but it must not return the tunnel's catch-all response. Browser and native mobile clients probe the registered capability origin before rendering, so incomplete DNS, TLS, or ingress configuration is shown as a preview error rather than a blank frame.

## Clients

The Electron desktop app can connect to a remote backend with a client URL or a pinned development backend:

```sh
JAZ_API_URL=https://jaz.example.com bun run dev
```

The browser client is a static web app. Host `frontend/dist-web` on any static host, for example `https://web.jaz.chat` or a self-hosted origin. It connects directly to the backend URL the user supplies; the backend is not involved in serving the web app.

An approved device can share a one-use enrollment link. To open it in the browser client, put its invitation in the fragment:

```text
https://web.jaz.chat/#server=https%3A%2F%2Fjaz.example.com&key=...
```


After a successful connection, the browser saves the backend URL in `localStorage` and the device credential encrypted in IndexedDB with a non-exportable AES-GCM key, bound to the backend origin. Refreshing the page revalidates the saved device with the server before reconnecting. Switching from `web.jaz.chat` to a self-hosted copy starts with separate browser storage. Forget removes the saved login; if site storage is unavailable, access lasts for the current page session.

Trusted browser origins may call a private or loopback backend, for example `http://localhost:5299`, as long as the browser allows the request. Jaz answers normal CORS preflights and Chrome Private Network Access preflights with `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true`.

Additional self-hosted browser origins must be explicitly listed with `--allowed-origins=https://app.example.com`. The public backend origin, Jaz web origins and loopback development origins are supported by default.

### Self-host the app and backend behind one origin (optional)

You only need this to reach the backend from a **browser** client. The Electron desktop app connects straight to a remote backend over plain HTTP, so it needs none of this — TLS and a reverse proxy matter only because a browser blocks an HTTPS page from calling a plain-HTTP backend (mixed content).

One HTTPS origin serves the web build at `/` and reverse-proxies the API to a backend that stays on `localhost`. The browser only talks to that origin (no mixed content, no CORS) and the backend is never exposed; the proxy is pure routing — requests still originate in the browser. This assumes the backend is already installed and running (see [Server Setup](#server-setup)).

**1. Pick the public hostname Caddy will serve.** It must resolve to the server, because Caddy auto-provisions a Let's Encrypt cert for it. With a domain, point an A record at the server IP. With only an IP and no DNS, use [sslip.io](https://sslip.io) — it resolves `<ip>.sslip.io` to `<ip>` for free:

```sh
HOST=34.9.55.98.sslip.io        # or your own domain: jaz.example.com
```

**2. Build the web app on the server.** Clone into `/opt/jaz` and build with `VITE_JAZ_API_URL=origin`, which makes the app use `window.location.origin` as its backend (so it targets whatever host serves it). Caddy serves the build in place — no copy step. Fits comfortably on a 2 GB VM:

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y git unzip
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash && export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH"
sudo git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/gluonfield/jaz.git /opt/jaz
sudo chown -R "$USER" /opt/jaz
cd /opt/jaz/frontend && bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts
POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN=<ph_project_token> \
  VITE_JAZ_API_URL=origin \
  bun run build:web                                         # builds /opt/jaz/frontend/dist-web
```

**3. Point the backend at loopback** so it stays private and Caddy is the only thing exposed:

```sh
sudo sed -i "s#^JAZ_ADDR=.*#JAZ_ADDR=127.0.0.1:5299#; s#^JAZ_PUBLIC_URL=.*#JAZ_PUBLIC_URL=https://$HOST#" /etc/jaz/jaz.env
sudo systemctl restart jaz
```

Keep `:5299` out of the firewall; open only `:80` and `:443`.

**4. Install Caddy and write the proxy config** (on the server; the heredoc substitutes `$HOST` and leaves Caddy's `{...}` placeholders alone):

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y caddy        # or download from caddyserver.com/download
sudo tee /etc/caddy/Caddyfile >/dev/null <<EOF
$HOST {
    @api path /v1/* /health
    handle @api {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:5299
    }
    handle {
        root * /opt/jaz/frontend/dist-web
        try_files {path} /index.html    # SPA fallback — serve index.html for client routes (/new, /sessions/…)
        file_server
    }
}
EOF
sudo systemctl reload caddy          # or run directly: sudo caddy run --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
```

Caddy provisions the cert on first start (needs `:80`/`:443` reachable) and upgrades websocket/SSE streams automatically.

Two lines in that `handle` block are load-bearing. **`try_files {path} /index.html` is the single-page-app fallback:** routes like `/new` or `/sessions/<id>` are client-side only — no such file exists on disk — so opening one directly or hard-refreshing it would 404 without this. `try_files` serves the real asset when the path matches a file and otherwise rewrites the request to `index.html`, letting the app's router resolve the route in the browser. It must come **before** `file_server`. And the `@api` block must stay **above** the web `handle` so `/v1/*` and `/health` reach the backend instead of falling through to `index.html`. Verify with `curl -sI https://$HOST/new | head -1` — it should report `200` and `Content-Type: text/html`, not `404`. The same fallback is required on any static host that serves the web build (nginx: `try_files $uri /index.html;`). Hosts that read a `_redirects` file — Cloudflare Pages, Netlify — are already covered: the build ships one at the deploy root (`frontend/src/renderer/public/_redirects` → `dist-web/_redirects`) with `/*  /index.html  200`.

**5. Verify and connect.**

```sh
curl -fsS https://$HOST/health        # -> {"ok":true,...}
```

## Connected Devices

Each installation has a random, revocable bearer credential, stored as a hash
on the server. Devices in Settings lists approved, pending and revoked devices.
Revoking a device closes its active streams and cancels its unused invitations.

**Add Device** produces a one-use enrollment invitation that expires in ten
minutes. The invitation sits in the link fragment and is exchanged for a separate
device credential. It carries no permanent root authority. Entering the base URL
instead creates a pending request that an approved device or server operator
must approve.

Pairing proof is sent in `X-Jaz-Pairing-Secret` and redeemed once for a fresh
credential. Browser event streams and embedded files use one-minute resource tickets
from the authenticated `/v1/auth/check` response. Native clients use Authorization
headers; browser WebSockets and the Chrome bridge use a WebSocket subprotocol. Durable `?key=` resource
authentication is rejected.

OAuth credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and bound to their account ID.
The separate 32-byte key defaults to `<root>/secrets.key`; `JAZ_SECRET_KEY_FILE`
can point to a protected external key file. Preserve that key with secured
backups: a database copy alone cannot restore connected accounts. Existing
plaintext OAuth rows are encrypted on startup and SQLite plaintext pages are
purged. The runtime directory is private and DB/WAL files use mode 0600.
Desktop credentials use the OS encryption service; iOS uses Keychain.

Upgrade the server and desktop client together, stopping the old server before
opening its database with the upgraded binary. Existing per-device credentials
continue to work. Unused invitations and resource tickets expire on restart.

# Bot artifact delivery

Bot chat now renders saved artifact events using the existing sandboxed `ArtifactBlock`. Previously the chat projection discarded these events and both history queries omitted them, while the tool told the agent the content had already been shown.

## Delivery contract

- History retains artifact events alongside the existing chat surfaces. Chat entries keep the source session, sequence and payload; replay uses the existing event coalescer.
- New artifact events record host acceptance for presentation. This marks turn delivery atomically with the saved event and keeps it visible on pages without turn context. It is not a client rendering acknowledgement.
- History resolves unmarked historical artifacts from bounded persisted message/activity predecessors in the same read transaction. The UI never infers visibility from a partial page. Unknown or conflicting same-millisecond provenance stays hidden; no migration or live transcript rewrite is needed.
- Artifact tools reuse the same session visibility rule as app presentations. Turns answering a peer bot or a group do not present into the user's bot chat.
- The MCP tool reports a saved artifact only after persistence succeeds. Missing sessions and failed writes cannot return success. The native tool reports preparation only. Neither claims the user has seen the result.
- Artifact prompt interactions return through the bot chat's existing send function.

## Child handoff using existing APIs

Creation in a child conversation does not present anything in its parent's chat. A saved event is addressed internally by its source session and sequence; there is no artifact registry or tool that presents an existing event by reference. `read_thread` exposes text and tool-name summaries, not artifact payloads. Full transcript HTTP history exposes the saved event payload.

The smallest supported handoff is a saved backend HTML/SVG file plus its source thread, path, title and short summary in the child's normal completion report. The parent can inspect the file through its filesystem tools or the existing session-file HTTP API, then call `visualise_show_widget` in the destination conversation. That tool currently requires `widget_code`; a filename or event reference alone does not render. This keeps raw code out of inter-agent report text, although the final presentation call still supplies it.

Use the existing file reader/preview proxy for a user-facing file link. A backend path is an agent-side reference, not an assumption that the client computer has that file. File references are mutable; include a content hash when a specific version matters. Keep the source thread/path or original event identity in the handoff report: the current presentation schema has no structured source-reference field.

This change adds no cross-conversation transport, gallery, artifact registry, new renderer or dependency.

Contract: `search({query})` returns `{results: [{id, title, url, text?}]}` as structured content ([OpenAI MCP docs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/mcp)). Jaz calls only tools named `search` that declare `readOnlyHint`, because it calls them on every debounced keystroke. `GET /v1/search/connections?q=` asks all such servers at once with a 5 s deadline and drops untitled results and non-web links. Sections arrive together, between Threads and Archived; a failing or slow server is left out and logged.

Tasks returns up to 10 issues (title; identifier, state and assignee as text). CRM returns 3 matches of each object, name matches first (record name; object name as text).

Verification: Go suites pass in all three repos; Jaz frontend 315 tests, typecheck and lint pass. The Jaz manager test runs real MCP servers and fails with the read-only guard or the link filter removed. End to end, this branch's backend in a scratch home searched a locally run, seeded Tasks server, and headless Chrome drove the real palette: the Tasks section rendered, arrow keys and Enter opened the issue URL, and an unmatched query showed "No matches". CRM was verified through its MCP test, not run locally.

Review: three thermo-nuclear passes, all by the implementing agent; an independent reviewer was interrupted twice and never reported. Fixes: CRM search builds results in one loop and always returns an array; failure logging skips requests the palette cancelled, judged from Jaz's own context. Declined: per-source progressive loading, which costs a sources endpoint and N requests for little gain with two fast servers; a shared cross-object query in CRM's records layer, since its MCP handlers already orchestrate service calls this way.

Opening in Jaz: each Tasks and CRM result carries OpenAI's MCP extensions preview target, `_meta["openai/preview"].target = {type: "mcp_app_tool", name, arguments}`: `show_tasks {view: "EE-1"}` or `show_crm {path: "/r/<id>"}`. Jaz keeps a target only when it names one of that server's sidebar (global entrypoint) apps and always sets the `app` field itself, so a server cannot supply it directly. Enter switches the left nav to that app and sends the target as a new call of its tool; the Tasks and CRM apps navigate on that input. Results without an app target still open their link. Verified end to end: Enter on a Tasks result opened the issue in the Tasks sidebar app, a second selection moved the open app to the next issue, and no browser tab opened. The Jaz test fails when the sidebar-app check or the host-owned `app` field is removed.

CRM ranking: text searches ordered matches newest first, so "Jim Mayer" returned three newer people whose notes mention him and cut off his own record. CRM's record query now ranks where the text matched: the name, then an email address or domain, then anything else, newest first within each. One lateral match computes both the filter and the rank. This also changes `search_records` with a text query and CRM's own palette. A records test fails with the ranking removed; live, "Jim Mayer" now returns his record first.
